did.abstract: The collection includes letters and photographs from Elizabeth Fenno Upton (VC 1903) to her friends and family that detail her life and work in Japan as a Christian missionary dedicated to early childhood education and social work.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Born in 1880 in Maine to Elizabeth Fenno Perry (1856-1885) and Francis Robbins Upton (1852-1921), Elizabeth Fenno Upton was an Episcopalian missionary and social worker. Her father, Francis Upton, was a physicist, mathematician, and engineer who worked closely with Thomas Edison. Elizabeth Upton graduated from Vassar College as part of the Class of 1903, alongside her life-long friend Elizabeth B. (Thompson) Reed, whom she affectionately addresses as "Ibbit" in many of her letters. After Vassar, Upton spent several years in Europe, studying at the Sorbonne (1905-1906) and the University of Berlin (1906-1907). In 1907, Upton moved to Japan as a Christian missionary, where she began charitable work with the poor and the sick, funded by her own family wealth and by donations.

Although she never married, Upton adopted a son, Yohane T. Kanai (b. 1909) when he was a baby. Yohane eventually married and adopted several children of his own, although he struggled with mental health problems his whole life and Elizabeth writes that he was eventually diagnosed with "dementia praecox."

Aside from spreading Christianity in Japan, Upton dedicated her life to teaching children and helping Japanese people in need, and her communities loved her in return. Upton’s professional accomplishments included opening over a dozen kindergartens in Saitama Prefecture, as well as a church called the Church of the Holy Spirit, notable for its embrace of societal "outcastes." Upton depended on American donors, many of whom were also Vassar alumnae, to fund her projects. After spending many years working in Japan, she eventually settled in Moroyama in 1934, and this is where she founded her church. Elizabeth spent periods of time living away from Japan in France and the United States, including from 1941 to 1947 due to WWII. She returned to Moroyama, however, and lived in Japan until the end of her life in July 1966 at age 86.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Content Note
scopecontent.p: The collection includes correspondence from Elizabeth Fenno Upton (1880-1966) to her friends and family, including her life-long friend Elizabeth B. (Thompson) Reed and Mary (Belknap) Gray, who were both Vassar classmates from the Class of 1903. Also included are photographs of Upton, her adopted son Yohane T. Kanai, her family and friends, and the communities with whom she worked while living in Japan. Upton's letters, particular those distributed to her wider circle of friends and donors, summarize the status of professional projects made possible by donor contributions, as well as include anecdotes about her life in Japan. These letters describe her work with the sick, particularly the mentally ill and those inflicted with tuberculosis and leprosy, and the poor, particularly children and orphans. The collection also contains a few printed written works by Upton on subjects such as motherhood, religion, and the treatment of mental illness in Japan.

acqinfo.head: Acquisition Information
acqinfo.p: Most of the collection, including photographs, was the gift of Anna (Reed) Dean (VC 1943), February 1966.
Additional correspondence was the gift of Mary (Belknap) Gray (VC 1903), November 1968.
